3. Learned counsel appearing for the parties submit that
all disputes and differences between the parties have
been amicably resolved and that the parties have decided
to  part  ways  amicably  on  the  terms  and  conditions
contained in the Settlement Agreement dated 09.11.2026.
Accordingly, it is prayed that appropriate and necessary
orders may be passed in terms thereof.
4. The  parties,  who  are  present  through  video
conferencing  mode,  are  duly  identified  by  their
respective learned counsel.
5. Through their counsel, the terms and conditions have
been specified and explained, and the parties have also
undertaken  to  stand  by  the  terms  of  the  Settlement
1

--- Page 32 ---
Agreement. It has also been explained that in case of
violation of any of the terms or non-compliance thereof,
the same will be termed as contempt of the Court and
proceedings could be initiated.
6. We appreciate the efforts taken by Ms. Kongara Vijaya
Lakshmi,  Former  Judge  of  the  High  Court  of  Andhra
Pradesh, who mediated the dispute between the parties. We
also appreciate the efforts put in by learned counsel
appearing for the parties.
7. The terms of the Settlement Agreement read as under:
“ 14. Payment to the Second Party
14.1 In full and final satisfaction of the direction
in  the  Tribunal's  Order  for  return  of  Rs.
1,63,35,600/-  (Rupees  One  Crore  Sixty-Three  Lakhs
Thirty-Five Thousand Six Hundred only), the First
Party shall pay the Second Party a total sum of Rs.
40,00,000/- (Rupees Forty Lakhs only), as follows:
(a) Rs. 30,00,000/- (Rupees Thirty Lakhs only), which
was  deposited  in  the  Second  Party's  Account  on
21.10.2026 pursuant to the order dated 28.09.2026; and
(b) the balance of Rs. 10,00,000/- (Rupees Ten Lakhs
only), has been given in the form of the cheque
bearing  Cheque  No.  000032  drawn  on  HDFC  Bank,
Peerzadiguda Branch in favour of the Second Party. The
aforesaid cheque has been handed over by Party No. 1
to the Second Party on the date of signing of this
Agreement.
14.2 The members of the First Party are jointly and
severally liable for the payment under clause 14.1(b).
2

--- Page 33 ---
14.3 The monthly amounts of Rs. 3,40,000/- paid to the
Second Party under the order dated 28.09.2026, up to
the date on which the Hon'ble Supreme Court disposes
of the SLPs in terms of this Agreement, belong to the
Second Party absolutely. They shall not be adjusted
against  the  sum  of  Rs.  40,00,000/-  and  are  not
refundable.
14.4 Time is of the essence for the payment under
clause 14.1(b). If it is not made in full by the due
date, the concession granted by the Second Party under
clause 14.1 shall stand withdrawn, and the direction
in  the  Tribunal's  Order  for  return  of  Rs.
1,63,35,600/- shall be enforceable against the First
Party in full, after giving credit only for the
amounts actually paid under clause 14.1.
15.  Properties  that  belong  to  the  Second  Party
absolutely
15.1 The following properties belong to the Second
Party absolutely ("Second Party's Properties"):
(a) Unit Nos. G2/A (Ground Floor), 105 (First Floor),
204 (Second Floor) and 205 (Second Floor) in ACE
CRYSTAL, more fully described in Schedule 'C' (the
"Schedule C Units"); and
(b) Unit No. 403 (Fourth Floor) in ACE CRYSTAL, more
fully described in Schedule C 'Item C-5' ("Unit 403");
and
(c) the Schedule B Property.
15.2 The First Party acknowledges that the Second
Party is the absolute owner of the Second Party's
Properties. The First Party relinquishes in favour of
the Second Party all rights, title, interest and
claims in the Second Party's Properties, whether under
the  Seven  Deeds,  the  Development  Agreement,  the
Supplementary Deed, the Lease Deed or otherwise, and
shall not make any claim to them at any time.
3

--- Page 34 ---
15.3 The Seven Deeds having been declared null and
void by the Tribunal's Order, as confirmed by the Writ
Appeal Judgment, and the Sub-Registrar having given
effect to the cancellation in the encumbrance records,
the Second Party's Properties stand re-vested in the
Second Party under her original title, namely the Gift
Settlement Deed bearing Document No. 6248/2003. The
First Party accepts this position. It is agreed that
to place the Second Party's title beyond doubt in the
records of the Sub-Registrar, the First Party shall,
within (15) days from the date of this Agreement,
execute  and  register  before  the  concerned  Sub-
Registrar a Deed of Relinquishment/Release, and/or
such other deed or agreement as may be appropriate, in
favour of the Second Party in respect of the Second
Party's Properties, namely the five units in Schedule
'C' and the Schedule B Property, relinquishing all
rights, title, interest and claims of the First Party
in them and confirming that they belong to the Second
Party absolutely. As regards the Plot 39 Property,
which also stands in the name of the Second Party
after  the  cancellation,  the  Second  Party  shall
relinquish her rights in it in favour of First Party
in the manner provided in clause 17.
15.4 The First Party shall hand over to the Second
Party all original title deeds and link documents
relating to the Second Party's Properties which are in
its possession, including the original Gift Settlement
Deed bearing Document No. 6248/2003, the Development
Agreement, the Supplementary Deed, the Lease Deed and
the Seven Deeds on the date of signing of this
Agreement.
15.5 Within (07) days from the date of this Agreement,
the  First  Party  shall  deliver  possession  of  the
Schedule B Property to the Second Party and shall not
interfere with it thereafter.
4

--- Page 35 ---
15.6 The First Party confirms that, except the Lease
Deed, no sale, mortgage, lease, charge, agreement or
other  encumbrance  or  third-party  right  has  been
created by or through the First Party in the Second
Party's Properties, and the First Party shall not
create any such encumbrance or right hereafter. If any
such encumbrance or claim comes to light, the First
Party shall, at its own cost, have it removed and
shall keep the Second Party indemnified against all
loss on that account. All property tax, maintenance
charges and other dues relating to the Second Party's
Properties up to the date of this Agreement shall be
borne by the First Party.
15.7 The First Party shall sign all applications,
affidavits, no-objection letters and other documents
required for mutation of the Second Party's Properties
in the name of the Second Party in the records of the
Greater  Hyderabad  Municipal  Corporation,  the
Mangalpally  Gram  Panchayat,  the  Sub-Registrar  and
every other authority, and shall render all assistance
required for the purpose at the cost of the second
party.
16. Lease Deed and rents
16.1 From the date of this Agreement, the rent payable
under the Lease Deed in respect of the Schedule C
Units belongs to the Second Party alone. Any rent or
income from Unit 403 from the date of this Agreement
also belongs to the Second Party alone.
16.2 Within (07) days from the date of this Agreement,
the First Party shall address a letter to the Lessee,
with a copy to the Second Party, informing the Lessee
that the First Party's share in the leased premises on
the ground, first and second floors of ACE CRYSTAL,
namely the Schedule C Units, now belongs to the Second
Party, and that the rent for those units shall be paid
5

--- Page 36 ---
directly to the Second Party's Account from the next

16.3 The First Party shall take all steps and execute
all documents, including any supplementary lease deed,
attornment letter or other communication, required by
the Lessee or any authority for substituting the
Second Party as lessor of the Schedule C Units.
16.4 Any rent received by the First Party in respect
of the Schedule C Units for any period after the date
of this Agreement shall be paid over to the Second
Party within (07) days of its receipt.
17. Properties that go to the First Party
17.1 That Plot No. 39 of the Schedule A Property,
together with the building constructed on it, more
fully  described  in  Schedule  'D'  (the  "Plot  39

accordance with their respective existing ownership
interests, within (15) days after the First Party has

(b)  simultaneously  when  the  necessary  deed(s)  in

all five ACE CRYSTAL units specified in Schedule 'C'
and the Schedule 'B' Property;
(c)  handing  over  of  all  original  documents  and
delivery of possession of the Schedule 'B' Property;
6

--- Page 37 ---
17.3 The Plot 39 Property are released on an "as is
where is" basis. The Second Party gives no warranty
regarding them and shall not be liable for any claim,

including  any  liability  under  the  Development

17.4 All stamp duty, registration charges and other

and for mutation under this Agreement, shall be borne

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
 
Civil Appeal No.2849 of 2022 
 
 
Insurance Regulatory and  
Development Authority of India                      
...Appellant 
 
Versus 
 
Alankit Insurance TPA Ltd.            
   ...Respondent 
 
O R D E R 
 
In the present appeal, we are concerned with the 
impugned order which remanded the matter of renewal of 
Certificate of Registration of the respondent herein, to the 
Authority, directing it to pass a fresh order in accordance with 
law, in the light of the observations made in the impugned order.  
2. We heard, Mr. N. Venkataraman, learned A.S.G. appearing 
for the appellant and Mr. Sudhir Makkar, learned Senior Counsel 
appearing for the respondent.  
3. Learned A.S.G. would contend that the Authority is only 
concerned with the observation made in the order which indicate 
that the TPA Regulations with respect to renewal are not 
mandatory. The learned Senior Counsel for the respondent, 

--- Page 78 ---
Page 2 of 5 
 
 
however, would assert that even if they are considered 
mandatory, the respondent satisfies the criteria.   
4. The Regulations are produced in the Appendix, is called 
the Insurance Regulatory & Development Authority of India (Third 
Party Administrators-Health Services) Regulations, 2016. The 
issue is with respect to the renewal of the Certificate of 
Registration of the respondent to act as a Third Party 
Administrator (TPA).  Admittedly, it was renewed for the period 
November 18, 2017 to November 17, 2020. On October 01, 2020, 
the appellant filed an application for renewal of the Certificate of 
Registration under Regulations 2015 which stood rejected for the 
Minimum Business Requirement (MBR) not being satisfied.  
5. The MBR, as seen from Regulation 14, requires compliance 
with minimum business norms towards health services for the 
insurers registered with the authority, as may be specified by the 
Authority from time to time, the services not reckoned for such 
minimum business norms being mentioned in the proviso. The 
non-compliance with MBR is stipulated in Regulation 15(C). As 
per Clause 6 of Regulation 15(C), if the MBR is not satisfied by a 
TPA, the same shall be decided in the manner provided under 

--- Page 79 ---
Page 3 of 5 
 
 
sub-clauses (a) to (b) and if that is not satisfied then under sub-
clause (c), there shall be no renewal.   
6. The consideration of the respondent TPA comes under sub-
clause (b) of Section 15 (c)(b), as admitted by both parties, which 
is extracted hereinbelow: - 
b. Where a TPA has failed to fulfil the minimum business 
requirements in any of the parameters specified in one 
financial year, but has met with the norms on an average 
basis for the years under consideration the Authority may 
consider the renewal based on the reasons furnished by 
the TPA. 
   
7. The learned A.S.G. also points out that the MBR of TPAs is 
brought out by the Authority, produced at Annexure A5, of which 
the following paragraph is relevant and extracted hereinbelow: - 
In respect of the applications received for the renewal of 
the certificate of registration, the business procured in the 
applicable preceding Financial Years shall be taken into 
consideration while determining the fulfilment of minimum 
business requirements in accordance to the provisions of 
Regulation 15 (C) (6). Where a TPA Company has 
completed more than six months business in a financial 
year and due for renewal, such TPA Company shall fulfil 
the proportionate business in respect of the completed 
number of months in that incomplete financial year. In 
case if a TPA Company has completed less than six 
months in a financial year and due for renewal, that 
period may be ignored.  
 

--- Page 80 ---
Page 4 of 5 
 
 
8. It is the submission of the Authority that when the renewal 
period extends beyond the six months period, in a financial year, 
the proportionate business in respect of completed number of 
months in that incomplete financial year shall be taken into 
account. Hence, the authority submits that insofar as the 
respondent is concerned though the earlier certificate was valid 
upto 17.11.2020, the consideration can be only with respect to 
policies serviced till 30.10.2020, since in the incomplete financial 
year, there are only seven completed months from April to 
October.  Even if such consideration is made, the MBR is satisfied, 
is the contention of the respondent.  
9. In this context, we also have to observe that the contention 
taken by the respondent, as noticed in the impugned order, is that 
there were 6,666 policies serviced on 27.10.2020 which were 
processed in November and December by the insurance 
company.       
10. Hence, if the premiums were paid and the policies were 
serviced by the respondent, necessarily these have to be 
reckoned which however will have to be considered by the 
Authority.  

--- Page 81 ---
Page 5 of 5 
 
 
11. In the above circumstances, we affirm the order of remand 
but however make it clear that the Authority shall consider the 
issue on the basis of the TPA Regulations which are mandatory in 
nature. However, it shall also be considered as to whether the 
policies or lives processed in the months of November and 
December 2020 were, in fact, serviced in October 2020. 
12. The appeal stands disposed of. 
13. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of. 
 
 
 
.......…….……………………. J. 
                       (J. B. PARDIWALA) 
 
 
 
....……….……………………. J. 
                                         (K. VINOD CHANDRAN) 
 
NEW DELHI; 
NOVEMBER 20, 2026.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA

(@ SLP (CIVIL) NO.22599 OF 2026) 
 
KANPUR DEVELOPMENT  
AUTHORITY                    …APPELLANT(S) 
VERSUS 
B.N. TRIPATHI & ORS.            …RESPONDENT(S) 
 
WITH 
CIVIL APPEAL NO………………………….OF 2026 
(@ SLP (CIVIL) NO.22644 OF 2026) 
 
O R D E R 
 
1. Leave granted. 
2. The present appeals arise from the judgment and order 
dated 09.04.2026 passed by the High Court of Judicature 
at Allahabad (hereinafter referred to as the “High Court”) 
in First Appeal No. 10 of 2022, whereby the High Court 
allowed the appeal preferred by the original plaintiffs and 
set aside the judgment and decree dated 20.04.2016 
passed by the Trial Court in Original Suit No. 243 of 2009. 
The said suit had been instituted seeking, inter alia, a 
decree of mandatory injunction for delivery of possession 
of Plot No. 56, Block-A, Scheme No. 39, Jajmau, Kanpur, 
along with damages and other consequential reliefs. 

--- Page 100 ---
C.A. NO……/2026 @ SLP(C) NO.22599/2026  
WITH CONNECTED  Page 2 of 6 
 
Aggrieved by the judgment of the High Court, the Kanpur 
Development Authority (hereinafter referred to as the 
“KDA”) and the State of Uttar Pradesh have preferred the 
present appeals. 
3. The facts giving rise to the present appeals are as follows: 
3.1. The dispute concerns Plot No. 56, Block-A, Scheme 
No. 39, Jajmau, Kanpur, admeasuring 2,222 square 
yards (hereinafter referred to as the “disputed plot”). 
The said plot was allotted to respondent No. 1, B.N. 
Tripathi, pursuant to an auction conducted in the 
year 1967. Subsequently, a registered lease deed 
dated 03.12.1984 was executed by the KDA in favour 
of respondent No. 1 and his wife, Smt. Yugrani Devi, 
for a period of 999 years. 
3.2. A dispute arose between the parties regarding 
delivery of physical possession of the disputed plot. 
The original plaintiffs claimed that despite execution 
of the lease deed and repeated requests, possession 
was never handed over to them. The KDA, however, 
maintained that possession had already been 
delivered. The parties had also been involved in 
earlier civil proceedings concerning the demand of 
interest and sanction of the building plan. 
3.3. The original plaintiffs thereafter instituted Original 
Suit No. 243 of 2009 seeking mandatory injunction 
for delivery of possession and damages of Rs. 

--- Page 101 ---
C.A. NO……/2026 @ SLP(C) NO.22599/2026  
WITH CONNECTED  Page 3 of 6 
 
41,16,800/- with interest. By judgment and decree 
dated 20.04.2016, the Trial Court dismissed the suit, 
holding that the plaintiffs had failed to establish their 
case regarding non-delivery of possession. 
3.4. Aggrieved thereby, the plaintiffs preferred First 
Appeal No. 10 of 2022 before the High Court. By the 
impugned judgment dated 09.04.2026, the High 
Court reversed the findings of the Trial Court and 
directed delivery of physical possession of the 
disputed plot. It further awarded damages of Rs. 
13,700/- per month from 01.07.1987 until delivery of 
possession, along with interest at the rate of 6% per 
annum, Rs. 5,00,000/- towards escalation in 
construction costs and exemplary costs of Rs. 
2,00,000/-. The High Court also issued directions in 
paragraph 58 concerning an inquiry into the conduct 
of the officials responsible for non-delivery of 
possession and recovery of damages from them. 
 
4. We have heard Mr. R. Venkataramani, learned Attorney 
General for India, appearing on behalf of the appellant, 
Kanpur Development Authority; Mr. K.M. Nataraj, 
learned Additional Solicitor General, appearing on behalf 
of the appellant, State of Uttar Pradesh; and Mr. Arvind 
Varma, learned senior counsel, appearing on behalf of the 
respondents. 

--- Page 102 ---
C.A. NO……/2026 @ SLP(C) NO.22599/2026  
WITH CONNECTED  Page 4 of 6 
 
5. On the joint request made by learned senior counsel 
appearing for the parties, the appeals have been taken up 
for final hearing at this stage. We have also carefully 
perused the material placed on record.  
6. Having considered the submissions advanced by learned 
counsel for the parties and the material placed on record, 
we are of the view that the impugned judgment calls for 
interference only to a limited extent. In view of the 
statement made by the learned Attorney General 
regarding delivery of possession of the disputed plot to the 
respondents, we do not consider it necessary to examine 
the rival claims concerning the earlier delivery of 
possession. The principal question which remains for our 
consideration is whether the award of damages and 
exemplary costs, along with the directions issued in 
paragraph 58 of the impugned judgment, can be 
sustained. 
7. Insofar as the award of damages is concerned, the High 
Court has proceeded primarily on the basis of the project 
report submitted by the original plaintiffs, which 
estimated a monthly profit of Rs. 13,700/- from the 
proposed business. Admittedly, the proposed factory was 
never established and the business never commenced. 
The anticipated profits mentioned in the project report 
could not, merely because they remained unrebutted, be 
treated as conclusive proof of the profits which the 

--- Page 103 ---
C.A. NO……/2026 @ SLP(C) NO.22599/2026  
WITH CONNECTED  Page 5 of 6 
 
plaintiffs would have earned over such an extended 
period. Similarly, the award of Rs. 5,00,000/- towards 
escalation in the cost of establishing the factory was not 
supported by sufficient evidence establishing the actual 
loss suffered under that head. We are, therefore, of the 
considered view that the award of damages under 
subparagraphs (B) and (C) of paragraph 61 of the 
impugned judgment cannot be sustained. 
8. We are also of the view that the directions contained in 
paragraph 58 of the impugned judgment, requiring an 
inquiry into the conduct of the concerned officials and 
recovery of damages from them, were not warranted in 
the facts and circumstances of the present case. The 
individual responsibility of the officials concerned was 
neither the subject matter of the civil suit nor 
independently adjudicated upon. The award of exemplary 
costs of Rs. 2,00,000/- under subparagraph (F) of 
paragraph 61, which proceeds on the same 
considerations regarding the alleged conduct of the 
defendants, also does not warrant being sustained. 
Accordingly, these directions and the award of exemplary 
costs are liable to be set aside. 
9. Accordingly, the appeals are partly allowed. The 
directions contained in paragraph 58 of the impugned 
judgment, as well as the reliefs granted under 
subparagraphs (B), (C) and (F) of paragraph 61 of the said 

--- Page 104 ---
C.A. NO……/2026 @ SLP(C) NO.22599/2026  
WITH CONNECTED  Page 6 of 6 
 
judgment, are hereby set aside. The remaining directions 
of the High Court shall remain undisturbed. 
10. In view of the statement given by the learned Attorney 
General, the possession of the disputed plot shall be 
handed over forthwith to the respondents. 
11. Pending applications, if any, stand disposed of.

--- Page 106 ---

implication of the appellant is based on
confessional statement and certain Whatsapp
communication, the veracity of which would
have to be tested in the trial. It has been
submitted that the appellant has suffered
nearly two years of incarceration pending
trial and the trial is not likely to be
concluded  in  near  future.  In  such
circumstances, the appellant is entitled to
be released on bail.

messages.

in the other criminal case also pertaining
to the offence under the NDPS Act, the
appellant was implicated on the basis of
confessional statement merely because he was
the  owner  of  the  truck  in  which  the
contraband was found under transportation.
7. Having regard to the facts of the
case, without expressing any opinion on the
merits thereof, we are of the view that the

C.A. No.14780-14781 of 2025 etc. 
 
 
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
 
Criminal Appeal Nos.4333 of 2026 
 
  
Golap Hussain    
...Appellant 
 
Versus 
 
The State of Assam & Anr.           
 ...Respondents 
 
O R D E R 
 
The appellant along with another, was accused of 
kidnapping, with intent to confine a minor child under Section 
365 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC) and committing rape 
on her, also charged under Section 4 of the Protection of 
Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 (POCSO Act). Two 
accused were arrayed before the Trial Court under Section 365 
read with Section 34 and Section 120(B) of the IPC and Section 
4 of the POCSO Act. The second accused was acquitted and the 
appellant was convicted to twenty years, with a fine of 
Rs.15,000/- and a default sentence of two years rigorous 
imprisonment. The High Court in appeal acquitted the 
convicted accused of the charge under Section 365 read with 
Section 34 of the IPC, confining the conviction to Section 4 of the 
POCSO Act. The High Court, while affirming the conviction, 

--- Page 112 ---
Page 2 of 5 
C.A. No.14780-14781 of 2025 etc. 
 
modified the sentence noticing the amendment to Section 4 
having been brought in only in the year 2019; the offence 
having been committed in 2018. The sentence was reduced to 
nine years against which the present appeal is filed.  
2. We heard Sri B. K. Sharma, learned Senior Counsel 
appearing for the appellant and Sri Ankit Roy, learned 
Advocate-on-Record appearing for the State. 
3. Before the Trial Court, six witnesses were arrayed; PW1-
the victim, PW2, PW4 and PW5 – uncle of the victim; who was 
the first informant, her father and mother respectively, PW3-
Doctor, who examined the victim and PW6-the Investigating 
Officer (IO). 
4. PW1, in her chief-examination said that the appellant, 
along with two to three boys, abducted her from her house late 
at night and took her to another place, where she was forcibly 
raped by the appellant, for three to four days. It was also stated 
that her family members, with help of police, rescued her from 
the custody of the accused. However, in cross-examination, she 
admitted that she knew the mobile number of the appellant, 
who was her teacher and she had visited his house twice. She 
also admitted that she gave statement before the Police that she 

--- Page 113 ---
Page 3 of 5 
C.A. No.14780-14781 of 2025 etc. 
 
had a love affair with the accused person since December, 2017 
and hence she eloped with him on 15.06.2018, at night. It was 
asserted that the relationship was known to her people, but that 
as of now she does not want to marry the accused.  
5. The statement made by her before the police was quite 
contrary to her deposition before Court. PW2-the first 
informant, who was also staying in the very same premises 
lodged an FIR about the missing of the victim. PW4 and PW5 
also spoke of the kidnapping and molestation but they were not 
privy to the crime proper and their testimony can only establish 
the fact that their child was missing from the house on the night 
of 15.06.2018. 
6. PW3 is the Doctor, who examined the victim on her 
production on 23.06.2018. It was deposed that genital 
examination of the victim revealed that her hymen had an old 
tear at the 6 O’clock position. The Doctor opined that the age of 
the girl is above 14 and for determination of exact age 
radiological investigation is necessary. 
7. It is pertinent that no radiological investigation was 
conducted to ascertain the exact age of the victim, despite the 
opinion expressed by the doctor. Before us, there is a birth 

--- Page 114 ---
Page 4 of 5 
C.A. No.14780-14781 of 2025 etc. 
 
certificate produced as Annexure P2, issued by the Department 
of Health Services under Section 12/17 of the Registration of 
Births and Deaths Act, 1969. However, there is an anomaly 
insofar as Ex.4, as evident from the deposition of the I.O is first 
stated to be the birth certificate and then as the sketch map 
prepared. Ex.7 is deposed to be the photocopy of the birth 
certificate; which copy definitely cannot be relied on. 
Obviously, if what is produced is a photocopy, it cannot be 
relied upon and in that event, there is nothing produced before 
the Court to indicate the date of birth.  
8. Be that as it may, even if accept the minority status of the 
victim, we cannot but find that the allegation of penetrative 
sexual assault as alleged under Section 4 of the POCSO Act has 
not been established. The statements given to the police as 
confronted in the cross-examination of the PW1-victim, as 
admitted by her, indicated that she had accompanied the 
appellant of her own free will and that they had no physical 
relations; the former being irrelevant if the victim is a minor.  As 
we noticed, the accused was acquitted of the charge of 
kidnapping by the Trial Court itself, the testimony of the 
prosecutrix does not commend us to convict the accused under 

--- Page 115 ---
Page 5 of 5 
C.A. No.14780-14781 of 2025 etc. 
 
Section 4 of the POCSO Act; especially since the statement 
confronted to her does not disclose any such penetrative sexual 
assault, which she admitted unequivocally and she denied any 
physical relationship.  
9. The appellant hence stands acquitted of the charges 
alleged against him and he shall be released forthwith if not 
required in any other case. If the appellant is already on bail 
then the bail bonds shall stand cancelled. 
10. The appeal is disposed of. 
11. Pending application (s), if any, shall stand rejected.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO(S).          OF 2026
     (@ SLP(C) NO(S). 16812/2026)
 
ASHOK RAM         ...Appellant
      VERSUS
THE STATE OF RAJASTHAN & ORS.          ...Respondents
 O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Despite notice having been served in pursuance of the
earlier order of this Court dated 06.08.2026, the detenue -
wife has not chosen to appear before this Court.
3. The present appeal has been filed against the impugned
order dated 14.10.2025, passed by the High Court of Judicature
for Rajasthan at Jodhpur in D.B. Habeas Corpus Petition No.
432/2025, whereby the High Court initiated criminal proceedings
against the appellant for filing a false affidavit before the
High Court.
4. The learned counsel appearing for the appellant submits
1

--- Page 122 ---
that the appellant is an illiterate person, and after making
efforts to trace the whereabouts of the detenue - wife, he
initially filed a complaint dated 15.08.2025. However, despite
the aforesaid efforts, the detenue could not be traced and
ultimately, a Habeas Corpus Petition No. 432/2025 was filed
before the High Court, when admittedly, the detenue was living
with her parents.
5. We have heard the learned counsel appearing for the
petitioner.
6. The issue before us is only with respect to the direction
issued in by the High Court to register an FIR against the
appellant for filing a false affidavit.
7.  We find force in the submissions of the learned counsel
appearing for the appellant, as it was the detenue, who left
the matrimonial home, a fact which has been duly recorded by
the Court in the impugned judgment itself. Therefore, the
appellant cannot be faulted for filing the Habeas Corpus
Petition.
8. In such view of the matter, the direction issued to
register the FIR against the appellant cannot be sustained.
Therefore, the impugned direction issued by the High Court to
register the FIR as well as the consequent direction to pay
2

--- Page 123 ---
maintenance of Rs. 1500/- per month each to the detenue and his
child,  stands  set  aside  particularly,  when  she  left  the
matrimonial home on her own volition.
9. We also take note of the fact that the detenue is not
willing to agitate her case before us, despite notice having
been served upon her.
10. In lieu of the aforesaid, the FIR filed in compliance of
the order of the Division Bench stands quashed.
11. The appeal stands allowed, accordingly.
12. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

                                        (M.M. SUNDRESH)
…………………………………………………J.

Leave granted.
The appellant seeks bail in connection with
FIR No.282/2025, dated 22.11.2025, registered at
Police Station - Sadar Chamab, District – Chamba,
Himachal Pradesh, for the offences punishable
under Sections 21 and 29 of the Narcotic Drugs
and  Psychotropic  Substances  Act,  1985  and
Sections  221 and  132 of  the Bharatiya  Nyaya
Sanhita, 2023.
We have heard the learned counsel appearing
for the parties.

--- Page 147 ---
2
Learned counsel appearing for the appellant
submitted  that  apart  from  the  period  of
incarceration undergone by the appellant, the
main accused himself has been granted bail. It is
further submitted that the appellant is a lady
and there are no prior criminal antecedents in
which the appellant is involved.
Learned counsel appearing for the respondent
- State submits that considering the nature of the
allegation, coupled with the recovery, there is no
need for interfere.
Having heard the learned counsel appearing
for the respective parties, suffice it to state
that apart from the fact that the appellant is a
lady, the main accused has already been granted
bail.  It  is  also  an  admitted  fact  that  the
appellant  has  been  under  incarceration  for  a
period of 11 months.
Considering the above, we are inclined to set
aside the impugned order and grant bail to the
appellant.

--- Page 148 ---
3
Accordingly, the impugned order stands set
aside and the appellant is granted bail on terms
and  conditions  to  the  satisfaction  of  the
concerned Trial Court.
The appeal stands allowed, accordingly.
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

Leave granted.
The appellant  seeks anticipatory  bail in
connection  with  FIR  No.259/2022,  dated
14.07.2022,  registered  with  Police  Station  –
Tappal, District – Aligarh, Uttar Pradesh, for
the offences punishable under Sections 147, 420,
467, 468 and 506 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.
We have heard the learned counsel appearing
for the parties.
Admittedly, the investigation is over and
the charge sheet has been filed way back in the
year  2022.  The  charges  could  not  be  framed
because one of the accused is absconding. 

--- Page 152 ---
2
Taking into consideration the fact that the
appellant is a lady and the charge sheet has been
filed in the year 2022 itself, there is no need
to arrest the appellant, as per the law clearly
laid down by this Court on earlier occasions. 
The subsequent issue for consideration is as
to whether the appellant would cooperate with the
conduct of trial. We have been informed that the
appellant,  pursuant  to  interim  protection
granted, has not appeared before the concerned
Trial Court on multiple occasions.
In such view of the matter, we are inclined
to grant anticipatory bail to the appellant, with
the observation that the concerned Trial Court
shall  pass  appropriate  orders  by  way  of  a
condition to secure the continued presence and
cooperation of the appellant before the Trial
Court during the course of trial. 
If the appellant is absent even after our
order granting anticipatory bail, it is well open
for  the  State  and  the  complainant  to  seek

--- Page 153 ---
3
cancellation  of  anticipatory  bail  before  the
concerned Trial Court.
Accordingly, the impugned order stands set
aside and the appellant is granted anticipatory
bail on the aforesaid terms, and also subject to
the terms and conditions which may be imposed by
the concerned Trial Court.
The appeal stands allowed, accordingly.
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

1. Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
3.This appeal arises from a judgment and
order dated 07.07.2026 passed by the High
Court  of  Madhya  Pradesh  at  Jabalpur
rejecting the regular bail prayer of the
appellant  in  connection  with  FIR  No.
167/2016,  registered  at  P.S.  Kotwali,
District Anuppur.
4. At the outset, learned counsel for
the  appellant  submits  that  the  offences
under which the appellant is being tried are
1

--- Page 157 ---
triable by a Court of Magistrate and by now
he  has  suffered  over  one  year  of
incarceration pending trial. Besides, co-
accused has been granted bail by this Court.
5. The  learned  Counsel  for  the  State-
respondent has opposed the prayer for bail
by  submitting  that  the  appellant  had
remained absconding for certain period and,
thereafter, has been apprehended. However,
he  could  not  dispute  that  by  now  the
appellant has suffered incarceration for a
period exceeding one year pending trial.   
6. Having regard to the fact that the
offences  are  triable  by  a  Court  of
Magistrate and the appellant has remained in
jail for a period exceeding one year, we are
of the view that the appellant is entitled
to be released on bail at this stage.
7. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed.
The order passed by the High Court rejecting
2

--- Page 158 ---
the regular bail prayer of the appellant is
set aside.
8. The appellant shall be released on
bail on such terms and conditions as the
trial court may deem fit to impose in the
facts and circumstances of the case.
9.Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall
stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(S).          OF 2026
     (@ SLP(Crl.) NO(S). 13188/2026)
 
JERAMBHAI NATHUBHAI GAMI & ORS.       ...Appellant(s)
     VERSUS
STATE OF GUJARAT & ANR.           ...Respondent(s)
 O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The present appeal has been filed challenging the order
dated 25.06.2026 passed by the High Court in Criminal Misc.
Application  (Recall)  No.8457/2026  in  Special  Criminal
Application No.11599/2023 by which the recall petition filed by
the private respondent(s) was allowed with a consequential
direction to restore the FIR being C.R. no. 11203030230525 of
2023 and all the consequential proceedings.
3. The learned counsel appearing for the appellants submits
that even assuming, that the compromise entered into between
the parties is not given effect to, the rigour under Section
362 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, which mandates the
court to not to alter or revise its judgment, save as otherwise
provided by the Code, would be applicable.  Furthermore, in
light of the judgment rendered by this Court in  Raghunath
Sharma vs. State of Haryana and Anr. 2025 SCC Online SC 1148,
the impugned judgment and order will have to be set aside.
4. The learned counsel appearing for the State and the
learned counsel appearing for the private respondent(s) submit
1

--- Page 174 ---
that  since  there  is  no  compliance  of  the  terms  of  the
compromise, and the earlier order of quashment having been
passed on the basis of settlement, the impugned order requires
no interference.
5. It is a settled principle of law that  fraud vitiates
every solemn act. In the present case, the quashment took place
only by virtue of a compromise entered into, between the
parties. Also, it is not the case of the appellant that the
terms of compromise have been implemented. Therefore, when a
party resiles from the statement made and received a benefit
from the Court, it is not open for him to later contend the
contrary, by taking an umbrage under the law.
6. In our considered view, Section 362 of the Code of
Criminal Procedure, 1973 would not come into play, especially,
on a perusal of the earlier order of the High Court dated
12.09.2023, quashing the criminal proceedings.
7. In view of the aforesaid findings, the decision rendered
by this Court in Raghnath Sharma (supra) also does not have any
application on the case at hand.
8. However,  we  are  inclined  to  set  aside  the  impugned
judgment of the High Court, only on the premise that after
recall of the quashing petition, it should have heard the
matter on merits, which has not been done in the present case.
9. Furthermore, taking into consideration the facts of the
case, we are inclined to hold that while the proceedings as
directed by the High Court shall be permitted to continue, no
final report shall be filed, till the disposal of the main
2

--- Page 175 ---
matter i.e., Special Criminal Application No.11599/2023.
10. We request the High Court to pass an appropriate order in
the aforesaid petition, within a period of eight weeks from the
date of receipt of a copy of this order, without being
influenced by the observations made in the impugned order and
the order passed by this Court.
11.  We further make it clear that till the disposal of the
main matter, the appellants need not surrender.
12. The appeal is disposed of, accordingly.
13. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
INHERENT JURISDICTION
REVIEW PETITION (Civil) No. 2671-2674/2025
(In C.A. Nos. 13250-13253/2024)
AJAY VERMA (DECEASED) THROUGH LR. ETC.             Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
ASHUTOSH MOHAN AGNIHOTRI & ORS.                    Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. Heard Mr. Amit Kumar Pathak, learned counsel appearing for the
review petitioners, and Ms. Aishwarya Bhati, learned Additional
Solicitor General appearing for the State.
2. The present review petitions call in question the correctness
of the order dated 26.11.2024, whereby this Court allowed the
appeal preferred by the State and set aside the order dated
10.05.2023 passed by the learned Single Judge directing the framing
of charges.
3. The review petitions have been filed primarily on the ground
that  during  the  proceedings  culminating  in  the  order  dated
26.11.2024, upon a query being posed by this Court, the learned
junior counsel appearing for the review petitioners (who were the
respondents in the main special leave petition) inadvertently
stated that pay fixation had indeed been effected for the review

--- Page 190 ---
2
petitioners on parity with one Shyamal Ganguly and Vimal Kumar
Upreti.
4. The learned counsel for the review petitioners submitted that
the said statement was factually inaccurate and that parity in pay
fixation was not, in fact, extended to the review petitioners with
those of Shyamal Ganguly and Vimal Kumar Upreti. Initially, when
the review petitioners approached the High Court by way of a writ
petition, the learned Single Judge, vide order dated 19.05.2004,
directed as under:
“In the result, the review petition as well as writ
petition,  insofar  as  it  relates  to  the  review
petitioners only are allowed. 
A  writ  in  the  nature  of  mandamus  is  issued
commanding the opposite parties to appoint the review
petitioners on the post of junior clerk, giving them
equal treatment which has been given to similarly
circumstanced persons, namely Shyamal Ganguly and Vimal
Kumar Upreti.”
5. The special appeal preferred against the said order was
subsequently disposed of, upon noting that the order passed by the
learned Single Judge stood complied with and had, by efflux of
time, rendered the appeal infructuous. Thereafter, a contempt
petition  was  filed,  which  was  disposed  of  by  recording  the
submission of the learned Standing Counsel for the State, which was
duly  concurred  in  by  the  learned  counsel  for  the  contempt
petitioners to the effect that the orders have been complied with.
6. Subsequently, in the second contempt petition, when charges

--- Page 191 ---
3
were directed to be framed, this Court was approached, which
culminated in the passing of the order dated 26.11.2024.
7. Having heard the learned counsel for the parties, we are
satisfied that not only before this Court, but even before the High
Court at the stage of the special appeal as also during the first
contempt proceedings, it was not disputed that the orders stood
fully implemented. At this distance of time, we cannot permit the
review petitioners to re-agitate or re-argue the matter on merits.
8. The review petitions are, accordingly, dismissed.
9. Pending applications, if any, stand disposed of.
......................J.
(K.V. VISWANATHAN)
......................J.
(ARUN PALLI)
NEW DELHI
NOVEMBER 2nd, 2026

1. By our order dated 12.10.2026, we had noticed that
eight parcels of land, which, the petitioner in the special
leave petition, submitted were ready for sale, for a total
amount of Rs.3,76,00,000/-. Today, we have been told by
1

--- Page 205 ---
Mr. Balbir Singh, learned Senior Counsel appearing for
respondent in the SLP that only two properties were sold and
the sale with respect to the remaining six have not been
proceeded  with.  The  learned  Counsel  appearing  for  the
petitioners  would  submit  that  the  sale  could  not  be
completed only due to the delay in sanctioning of loan by
the banks. As of now, the loan has been sanctioned and it is
submitted that within two weeks, definitely, the sale would
be completed.
2. We hence direct that the earlier procedure as required
by us shall be followed in the sale of the said properties
by the Principal District Judge (PDJ), Mysuru who has been
appointed as a Receiver of the properties.
3. We had also directed by the aforesaid order that seven
properties shall be auctioned within a period of three
months  from  the  date  of  that  order  and  had  directed
Rs.5,00,000/- to be retained with the PDJ to defray the
expanses  from  the  auction.  We  had  also  directed
Rs.4,52,86,000/-, which was remaining with the PDJ to be
disbursed to the respondent in the SLP. We see that the
respondent admits to have received Rs.4,57,86,000/-, the
entire amount, which remained with the PDJ as on the date of
the earlier order. We would require the PDJ to inform us as
to why the Rs.5,00,000/- as directed by us, to defray
expanses of auction, was not retained with the PDJ itself.
4. Mr. Balbir Singh, learned Senior Counsel had also
pointed out that the six properties, which had remained
2

--- Page 206 ---
unsold was to fetch a total amount of Rs.2,58,00,000/-; the
average selling price of which would be Rs.3,622.58/- per
sq. ft. It is also submitted by Mr. Balbir Singh, learned
Senior Counsel on behalf of the respondent in the SLP that
the respondent is ready to purchase the said properties at
an amount of Rs.4,000/- per sq. ft. Hence, we make it clear
that if the properties are not sold within the two weeks
stipulated hereinabove, then we would pass further orders on
the proposal made by the respondent in the SLP.
5. By the next posting date, we require the PDJ, Mysuru to
file a report as to the disbursement made by her and specify
why the Rs.5,00,000/- retention as directed by us was not
carried out as also indicate the status of the amounts with
respect to the two properties said to have been sold
pursuant  to  our  earlier  order.  The  sale  carried  out
hereafter and the steps for auctioning the properties also
shall be informed to us.
6. List the matter on 07.12.2026.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
 
CIVIL APPEAL NO.11994 OF 2026 
 
 
The State of Jharkhand & Ors.                               ...Appellants 
 
 
Versus 
 
Shahnaz Khatoon                                                   ...Respondent 
 
O R D E R 
 
We find absolutely no reason to interfere with the 
impugned order, especially since the State has been 
granted liberty to approach the Civil Court of competent 
jurisdiction. 
2. Learned Counsel appearing for the State of Jharkhand 
would point out that the learned Single Judge had directed 
the appellant-State to initiate acquisition proceeding of the 
land and pay a suitable compensation in lieu thereof, which 
has not been interfered with by the Division Bench. 
3. The controversy arose insofar as a pond existing in the 
subject property, sought to be renovated by the State 
Government, which was also alleged to be in public use. 
The respondent, however, claimed title over the property 
by virtue of a Sada Hukumnama executed in the year 1944. 
Learned Single Judge found that the pond was intended for 

--- Page 211 ---
Page 2 of 3 
 
 
the use of public at large and directed acquisition of the 
same, endorsing the title claimed by the writ petitioner who 
is the respondent herein. The Division Bench noticed that 
the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, empowered the Collector 
to conduct an inquiry with respect to disputes regarding the 
settlement of land, if such settlement is made on or after 
01.01.1946; while the Sada Hukumnama, relied on by the 
respondent herein was of the year 1944.  Hence, the liberty 
granted to the State to file a civil suit. 
4. We find that there is some anomaly insofar as the 
specific direction for acquisition made by the learned 
Single Judge having not been interfered with. To harmonize 
the two orders, we would only direct that the State may take 
any of the remedies; either proceed for acquisition or file a 
civil suit. However, filing of a civil suit cannot be kept 
pending endlessly.  Hence, if the State desires, the suit shall 
be filed within a period of six months from the date of this 
order, and the State also would be entitled to seek 
appropriate interim orders in the civil suit filed. However, if 
the State does not initiate the suit within the period 
provided, then necessarily the appellant can assert his title 
over the property and proceed further. In which event, the 

--- Page 212 ---
Page 3 of 3 
 
 
State can take over the pond and concede it to public use 
only if acquisition proceedings are taken. 
5. We make it clear that if a civil suit is filed, the same 
shall be considered on its own merits, in accordance with 
law. 
6. The appeal is disposed of. 
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.

1. Repeated orders have been passed by this Court to

till 30.10.2026.

appearing for the Bar Council of State of the Telangana
submits that an incorrect statement was made before the
Court, which came to be recorded in the order dated
09.10.2026, to the effect that the Interim Enrollment
Committee had already been constituted. He submits that

vide order dated 09.10.2026 and the earlier orders passed
in the matter.

meantime, the Interim Enrollment Committee has enrolled
2

more than 2,450 applicants as advocates. He submits that,

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
Leave granted. 
2. We have before us an appeal by a convict, who has
served almost 17 years with remission. The conviction
and sentence was upheld upto this Court. The appellant
prayed for parole before the High Court of Madhya
Pradesh which was declined by both the learned Single
Judge and the Division Bench.

--- Page 289 ---
3. We  heard,  Mr.  Vaibhav  Srivastava,  learned  Counsel
appearing for the appellant and Ms. Manisha T. Karia,
learned Senior A.A.G.  appearing for the respondent-
State. 
4. We had already granted parole to the appellant on
medical grounds projected of Carcinoma; Prostate with
Bone  Metastasis,  by  order  dated  16.07.2026.  We
directed the State to consider his case for remission
and in the meanwhile to produce a report of his
conduct during incarceration.
5. The affidavit filed in compliance of our order dated
16.07.2026 indicates that the appellant’s case does
not call for remission since the actual sentence
suffered by the appellant is 12 years, 6 months and 20
days, including the period spent in custody as an
undertrial. While the policy of the Government in
granting remission required completion of 14 years of
actual  imprisonment  and  20  years  of  imprisonment
including remission. 
6. A representation has been submitted by the appellant
to the Government of the State of Madhya Pradesh under
Article 161 of the Constitution of India which has
been forwarded by the Superintendent, Central Jail,
Bhopal  to  the  District  Magistrate,  Rajgarh  for
opinion. The State shall expedite the consideration of
the above representation. In the meanwhile, we noticed
that there is some discrepancy with respect to the age
of the appellant which is stated to be 69 years, 7
months and 3 days as on 22.07.2026. However, we notice
from the health report of the medical dispensary
produced as R7 that the age of the appellant is 79
years Annexure R9, the communication issued by the

--- Page 290 ---
office of the Superintendent, Central Jail, Bhopal in
the note sheet extracted indicates the age of the
appellant to be 71 years. 
7. We also noticed a decision of this Court in Writ
Petition (Crl.) No.162 of 2025, filed by the National
Legal  Services  Authority.  Therein  there  was  a
direction to all the States and Union Territories to
formulate and notify a comprehensive policy for early
or premature release of prisoners who are of advanced
age and/or are terminally ill; providing a clear and
unified definition of terminal illness.
8. Considering the entire facts and circumstances, we
deem it fit that the appellant be continued on parole,
awaiting the implementation of the policy, as directed
by this Court or consideration of the representation
made  by  the  appellant  under  Article  161  of  the
Constitution of India.  
9. List the matter after three months i.e. on 22.02.2027.
 (VISHAL ANAND)                                   (POOJA SHARMA)

THE APPLICATION FOR SETTING ASIDE THE ABATEMENT

Date : 20-11-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM :  HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE DIPANKAR DATTA
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE SHEEL NAGU
For Petitioner(s) :Mr. Tushar Mehta, Solicitor General
                   Ms. Manisha Lavkumar, Sr. Adv.
                   Ms. Deepanwita Priyanka- 2618, AOR
                   Mr. Aman Mehta, Adv.
                   Mr. Anuj Chaudhary, Adv.
                   
                   
For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. A  Division  Bench  of  the  High  Court  of  Gujarat,  vide order  dated  9th
September, 2024, has declined the prayer of the petitioners - State of Gujarat
and one of its officers - seeking condonation of 2028 days’ delay in presenting a
1

--- Page 292 ---
special appeal1, resulting in the same being dismissed as time-barred.
2. The  order  declining  condonation  of  delay  is  the  subject  matter  of
challenge in this special leave petition.
3. While the special appeal presented before the High Court was barred by a
huge delay, it is found that this special leave petition too is barred by 321 days
delay; also, there is a refiling delay of 240 days.
4. When a high court declines condonation of delay, the minimum this Court
would  expect  is  that  the  special  leave  petition  challenging  such  order  be
presented within the period of limitation prescribed for it so that the same can
be examined on merits. The right of appeal, no doubt, is a substantive right;
but, in a case of this nature, such right must be exercised within the prescribed
period of limitation, or at least briefly thereafter, if reasons beyond the control
of  the  party  seeking  condonation  of  delay  have  prevented  its  timely
presentation and sufficient cause is shown for such condonation.  A belated
exercise of that right, without an acceptable explanation, would defeat the very
purpose of the law of limitation.
5. Having regard to the decisions of this Court in Sheoraj Singh Vs. Union
of India2, Shivamma Vs. Karnataka Housing Board3, and State of Odisha
& Ors. Vs. Managing Committee of Namatara Girls High School4, we see
no  good  reason  to  condone  the  delay  in  presentation  of  the  special  leave
petition. 
8. The special leave petition stands dismissed as time-barred. 
9. Connected applications, too, stand dismissed.
1 LPA No.22193/20242 (2023) 10 SCC 5313 2025 SCC OnLine SC 19694 2026 INSC 148
2

--- Page 293 ---
10. We hope and trust that, drawing guidance from this order, the petitioners
would evolve a mechanism so that a proposal to challenge an order declining
condonation  of  delay  does  not  have  to  pass  through  several  channels  for
approval and that approval  granted by one  senior/responsible  officer would
suffice to facilitate presentation of a special leave petition within time. 
  (RASHMI DHYANI PANT)                       (SUDHIR KUMAR SHARMA)

3 and 4 of the application which reads thus:-
“3. That there has been delay in filing the present special leave petition
against the impugned judgment dated 07.11.2017. The unintentional
and inadvertent delay has been caused in filing the present Special
Leave Petition for the reasons that after receiving the certified copy of
the impugned judgement, the same was sent to Legal Remembrance &
Secretary to Government of Haryana, Law & Legislative Department for
giving his opinion as to whether the order of the Hon'ble High Court can
·be challenged by filing Special Leave Petition before this Hon'ble Court.
The office of the Legal Remembrance & Secretary to Govt. of Haryana
opined for challenging the order of the High Court in the instant case
before this Hon'ble Court and the same was forwarded to the office of
Advocate General, Haryana for taking necessary action for filing Special
Leave Petition. The petitioner thereafter requested the Ld. Advocate
General, Haryana for filing SLP before this Hon'ble Court. Thereafter the
office  of  Advocate  General,  Haryana,  forwarded  the  same  to  the
Haryana Legal Cell at New Delhi after appointing the Advocate for filing
the Special Leave Petition in the instant case.
4. That thereafter the complete case file was handed over to the office
of Additional Advocate General for drafting of Special Leave Petition in
the instant case. In this entire process for taking steps at different levels,
delay has occurred in filing the Special Leave Petition.”
3. Perusal of the same would indicate that it is as vague,  vagueness could
be and bereft of any material particulars. In a routine manner the delay is
sought to be explained which would not inspire confidence in this Court to
accept the same to be in the proximity of truth.
2

--- Page 317 ---
4. No doubt, litigant would not stand to benefit by approaching the Court
belatedly. However, the mere fact that cause brought to the notice of the Court
after considerable delay, without satisfactorily explaining the same, would not
constitute sufficient cause for condonation of delay. Hence, on the ground that
delay has not been satisfactorily explained, we dismiss the application and,
consequently, the Special Leave Petition as well.
5. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
    (DEEPANSHU)                          (AVGV RAMU)
SENIOR PERSONAL ASSISTANT             COURT MASTER (NSH)

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
Heard learned counsel appearing for the parties and
perused the material available on record. 
The petitioner has assailed the common judgment dated
19.10.2023 passed by the Division Bench of High Court of
judicature at Patna in LPA No.1376/2019 and 1408/2019.
The said litigation arose from the selection process
initiated in the year 2008, for appointment to the post of
Principals in Sanskrit Colleges in the State of Bihar.
It is not in dispute that writ petitions challenging the
alleged  irregularities  and  illegalities  in  the  said
selection process came to be instituted in the year 2011.
The petitioner who claims to have been unjustly deprived of
selection, did not challenge the decision of the Selection
Committee at that point of time.
For the first time, the petitioner approached the Writ
Court by filing an application for intervention in the year
2

--- Page 329 ---
2018, which was not favourably considered. 
In the Letters Patent Appeal, the petitioner moved an IA
for  intervention,  which  was  rejected  by  order  dated
30.01.2023, which the petitioner never challenged. 
The Division Bench dealt with the case of petitioner at
paragraph  no.21  of  the  impugned  order  observing  that
admittedly the intervenor also did not fare well in the
selection and failed to keep the standard for coming higher
up in the merit list. He had not challenged the selection
process and his intervention application had been dismissed
by the Division Bench with no further challenge to such
rejection. 
In this view of the matter, we are of the opinion that at
this belated stage, when many of the selected candidates
have already retired, the petitioner who was not even
allowed to intervene in the proceedings before the High
Court, cannot be permitted to lay challenge to a selection
process conducted way back in the year 2008.
The special leave petition lacks merit and is dismissed
as such.
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
(SACHIN)                                     (AKSHAY KUMAR BHORIA)

in C.A. No. No. 15391/2025 passed by the Supreme Court of India]
PEPSU ROAD TRANSPORT CORPORATION PATIALA           Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
ANU SUIA                                           Respondent(s)
 
Date : 20-11-2026 This petition was called on for hearing today.
CORAM :  HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE SATISH CHANDRA SHARMA
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE NONGMEIKAPAM KOTISWAR SINGH
For Petitioner(s) :By Courts Motion, AOR
                   Mr. K. K. Mohan- 289, AOR
                   
For Respondent(s) :Mr. Yadav Narender Singh- 2004, AOR
                   Mr. Mayank Kumar Singh, Adv.
                   Mr. Mudit Bansal, Adv.
                   
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Learned counsel appearing for the petitioner is
granted one week’s time to file an appropriate application
for bringing the legal heirs on record and to furnish the
bank account details of the legal heirs.
2. The  office  report  indicates  that  the  amount
deposited in the present matter has been kept in a non-
interest-bearing account. This Court fails to appreciate
why amounts deposited pursuant to the orders passed by this
1

--- Page 538 ---
Court are being retained in non-interest-bearing accounts.
3. Accordingly, the Secretary General of this Court is
directed to ensure that all amounts deposited pursuant to
the orders passed by this Court are, henceforth, kept in
interest-bearing  Fixed  Deposit  Receipts  (FDRs)  with
nationalised  banks,  on  an  auto-renewal  basis,  at  the
highest applicable rate of interest, so as to ensure that
the interest accrued thereon also enures to the benefit of
the rightful beneficiary.
4. The aforesaid directions shall be complied with
forthwith. Further, all amounts presently lying in non-
interest-bearing accounts shall be transferred to interest-
bearing Fixed Deposit Receipts (FDRs) within a period of
seven days from today.
5. List the matter after one week.
  (RAHUL KUMAR)                                    (KOMAL)
COURT MASTER (SH)                             COURT MASTER (NSH)

[Arising out of impugned final judgment and order dated 02-07-2026
in WA No.151/2025 passed by the High Court of Karnataka at
Bengaluru]
THE PROJECT DIRECTOR, 
NATIONAL HIGHWAYS AUTHORITY OF INDIA Petitioner
                                VERSUS
NARASIMHAMURTHY & ORS.                             Respondents
I.A. No.345054/2026-CONDONATION OF DELAY IN FILING
I.A. No.345055/2026-EXEMPTION FROM FILING O.T.
 
Date : 20-11-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM :  HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE DIPANKAR DATTA
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE SHEEL NAGU
For Petitioner(s) : Mr. Preetesh Kapur, Sr. Adv.
                    Mr. Sumit Gupta, Adv.
                    Mr. Pulkit Kaushik, Adv.
                    Ms. Ishant Tripathi, Adv.
                    Mr. Kartikeya Singh- 3570, AOR
                                      
For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. We have serious reservation with regard to the observation of the High
Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru1 in the impugned judgment and order dated
02nd July, 20262 that Section 16(2) of the National Highways Authority of India
Act,  19883 prescribes  that  for  the  purpose  of  public  amenities,  an  area  of
approximately one hectare of land i.e. 10,000 square meters of land has to be
1 High Court
2 impugned order
3 NHAI Act
1

--- Page 566 ---
acquired. Section 16(2) contains no such stipulation. We further do not approve
the direction of the High Court quashing the impugned notification in its entirety
when  the  respondent  no.1,  Narasimhamurthy,  had  prayed  for  the  following
limited relief:
“a. Issue a writ of certiorari or any other writ and quash the
Notification No.S.O.2460(E) Dated: 06-06-2023 Dated: 28-6-
2023 (sic, 27-6-2023) in respect of 0.10 guntas in Sy no.19/1
of  Koramanagala  Village,  Soluru  Hobli,  Magadi  Taluk,
Ramanagara  District  and  the  notice  dt.  5-7-2023,
No.SLAO&C.A/NH-48/C.R/11/2023-24 and [vide ANNEXURE A &
A1]”.
3. Be that as it may, we also find it inappropriate for the petitioner to acquire
the remaining land of the respondent 1, measuring 10 guntas, by the impugned
notification  particularly  when  his  property  measuring  approximately  26.08
guntas of land had already been acquired under the provisions of the NHAI Act
in the year 2007. The guidelines of the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways
dated 11th  February, 2021 should not have been deviated from, in the given
facts and circumstances.
4. We  dispose  of  this  special  leave  petition  with  a  modification  of  the
impugned order. It is observed that quashing of the impugned notification and
notice shall be restricted only to the prayer of the respondent no.1, extracted
supra,  more  particularly  the  land  in  village  Koramangala  described  in  the
notification and notice under challenge before the High Court.
5. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.
      (MANIK KUMAR)                         (SUDHIR KUMAR SHARMA)
SENIOR PERSONAL ASSISTANT                     COURT MASTER (NSH)

         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE DEVENDRA KUMAR UPADHYAYA

                   Mr. Raj Singh Phogat, Adv.
                   Mr. Kanchan Kumar Jha, Adv.
                   
                   
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
The impugned order has been passed on the basis of
earlier judgment of the Division Bench of the High Court in
“Rakesh Meghwal vs. State of Rajasthan & Ors”.
A perusal of the said judgment would reveal that the
1

--- Page 720 ---
Division Bench followed the view taken in “Manoj Kumar Sharma
vs. State of Rajasthan & Ors.”, in D.B. Civil Writ Petition
No.4637/2025 decided on 21.07.2025 in which, it was held that
amendment to Rule 25(2), insofar as it requires a minimum of
36% marks in each paper and 40% marks in the aggregate of the
written  examination,  is  not  a  fresh  amendment  but  a
clarificatory/correctional provision introduced to remove an
existing anomaly. 
The said judgment of the High Court in the case of Manoj
Kumar Sharma (supra) was challenged in “Hansraj Meena & Ors.
vs. State of Rajasthan” in SLP (C) 31931-31932/2026, which
has been dismissed by Co-ordinate Bench of this Court vide
order dated 16.09.2026.
Hence, we find no reason to entertain the instant special
leave petition which is dismissed as such. 
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of. 
 
(SACHIN)                                      (AKSHAY KUMAR BHORIA)
COURT MASTER (SH)                             COURT MASTER (NSH)
